listen_text: Chapter. The Sequent Calculus. Editorial note. This chapter presents Gentzen's standard sequent calculus LK for classical first-order logic. It could use more examples and exercises. To include or exclude material relevant to the sequent calculus as a proof system, use the “prfLK” tag. End chapter.

Section. Rules and derivation. For the following, let first Gamma, then capital Delta, then capital Pi, and finally capital Lambda represent finite sequences of sentences. Definition. Title: Sequent. A sequent is an expression of the form antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta where Gamma and capital Delta are finite (possibly empty) sequences of sentences of the language L . Gamma is called the antecedent, while capital Delta is the succedent. Explanation. The intuitive idea behind a sequent is: if all of the sentences in the antecedent hold, then at least one of the sentences in the succedent holds. That is, if Gamma equals the finite sequence first formula A sub one, continuing through the omitted intermediate entries, and finally formula A sub m and capital Delta equals the finite sequence first formula B sub one, continuing through the omitted intermediate entries, and finally formula B sub n , then antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta holds iff the conditional whose antecedent is open parenthesis, the conjunction beginning with formula A sub one, continuing through the omitted intermediate conjunctions, and ending with formula A sub m, close parenthesis; and whose consequent is open parenthesis, the disjunction beginning with formula B sub one, continuing through the omitted intermediate disjunctions, and ending with formula B sub n, close parenthesis holds. There are two special cases: where Gamma is empty and when capital Delta is empty. When Gamma is empty, i.e., m equals zero , antecedent containing no formulas; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta holds iff the disjunction beginning with formula B sub one, continuing through the omitted intermediate disjunctions, and ending with formula B sub n holds. When capital Delta is empty, i.e., n equals zero , antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing no formulas holds iff the negation of open parenthesis, the conjunction beginning with formula A sub one, continuing through the omitted intermediate conjunctions, and ending with formula A sub m, close parenthesis does. We say a sequent is valid iff the corresponding sentence is valid. If Gamma is a sequence of sentences, we write first Gamma, then formula A for the result of appending formula A to the right end of Gamma (and first formula A, then Gamma for the result of appending formula A to the left end of Gamma ). If capital Delta is a sequence of sentences also, then first Gamma, then capital Delta is the concatenation of the two sequences. Definition. Title: Initial Sequent. An initial sequent is a sequent of one of the following forms: Begin list. Next item. antecedent containing formula A; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A antecedent containing falsum; sequent arrow; succedent containing no formulas for any sentence formula A in the language. derivations in the sequent calculus are certain trees of sequents, where the topmost sequents are initial sequents, and if a sequent stands below one or two other sequents, it must follow correctly by a rule of inference. The rules for the sequent calculus L K are divided into two main types: logical rules and structural rules. The logical rules are named for the main operator of the sentence containing formula A and/or formula B in the lower sequent. Each one comes in two versions, one for inferring a sequent with the sentence containing the operator on the left, and one with the sentence on the right.

listen_text: Section. Quantifier Rules. Subsection. Rules for universal quantifier . Rule definition. Premise. antecedent containing first formula A with argument term t, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left universal quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument constant a Rule label: right universal quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x End displayed proof. In left universal quantifier rule, term t is a closed term (i.e., one without variables). In right universal quantifier rule, constant a is a constant which must not occur anywhere in the lower sequent of the right universal quantifier rule. We call constant a the eigenvariable of the right universal quantifier rule inference. Footnote. We use the term “eigenvariable” even though constant a in the above rule is a constant. This has historical reasons. End footnote. Subsection. Rules for existential quantifier . Rule definition. Premise. antecedent containing first formula A with argument constant a, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left existential quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first for some variable x, formula A with argument variable x, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t Rule label: right existential quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then for some variable x, formula A with argument variable x End displayed proof. Again, term t is a closed term, and constant a is a constant which does not occur in the lower sequent of the left existential quantifier rule. We call constant a the eigenvariable of the left existential quantifier rule inference. The condition that an eigenvariable not occur in the lower sequent of the right universal quantifier rule or left existential quantifier rule inference is called the eigenvariable condition. Explanation. Recall the convention that when formula A is a formula with the variable x free, we indicate this by writing formula A with argument variable x . In the same context, formula A with argument term t then is short for the result of substituting term t for variable x in formula A . So we could also write the right existential quantifier rule as: Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then the result of substituting term t for variable x in formula A Rule label: right existential quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then for some variable x, formula A End proof diagram. Note that term t may already occur in formula A , e.g., formula A might be atomic formula P applied to term t, then variable x . Thus, inferring antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then for some variable x, atomic formula P applied to term t, then variable x from antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then atomic formula P applied to term t, then term t is a correct application of right existential quantifier rule—you may “replace” one or more, and not necessarily all, occurrences of term t in the premise by the bound variable x . However, the eigenvariable conditions in right universal quantifier rule and left existential quantifier rule require that the constant a does not occur in formula A . So, you cannot correctly infer antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then for every variable x, atomic formula P applied to constant a, then variable x from antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then atomic formula P applied to constant a, then constant a using right universal quantifier rule . Explanation. In right existential quantifier rule and left universal quantifier rule there are no restrictions on the term t . On the other hand, in the left existential quantifier rule and right universal quantifier rule rules, the eigenvariable condition requires that the constant a does not occur anywhere outside of formula A with argument constant a in the upper sequent. It is necessary to ensure that the system is sound, i.e., only derives sequents that are valid. Without this condition, the following would be allowed: Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing formula A with argument constant a; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant a Rule label: *left existential quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for some variable x, formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant a Rule label: right universal quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for some variable x, formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing formula A with argument constant a; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant a Rule label: *right universal quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing formula A with argument constant a; sequent arrow; succedent containing for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x Rule label: left existential quantifier rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for some variable x, formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x End proof diagram. However, antecedent containing for some variable x, formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x is not valid.

listen_text: Section. Structural Rules. We also need a few rules that allow us to rearrange sentences in the left and right side of a sequent. Since the logical rules require that the sentences in the premise which the rule acts upon stand either to the far left or to the far right, we need an “exchange” rule that allows us to move sentences to the right position. It's also important sometimes to be able to combine two identical sentences into one, and to add a sentence on either side. Subsection. Weakening. Rule definition. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula A, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: right weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A End displayed proof. Subsection. Contraction. Rule definition. Premise. antecedent containing first formula A, then formula A, and finally Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left contraction rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula A, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A, and finally formula A Rule label: right contraction rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A End displayed proof. Subsection. Exchange. Rule definition. Premise. antecedent containing first Gamma, then formula A, then formula B, and finally capital Pi; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left exchange rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first Gamma, then formula B, then formula A, and finally capital Pi; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A, then formula B, and finally capital Lambda Rule label: right exchange rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula B, then formula A, and finally capital Lambda End displayed proof. A series of weakening, contraction, and exchange inferences will often be indicated by double inference lines. The following rule, called “cut,” is not strictly speaking necessary, but makes it a lot easier to reuse and combine derivations. Rule definition. Premise or initial sequent: antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A. Premise or initial sequent: antecedent containing first formula A, then capital Pi; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Lambda. The next inference is labeled cut rule. From the two immediately preceding branches using the cut rule, infer antecedent containing first Gamma, then capital Pi; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then capital Lambda. listen_text: Section. derivation. Explanation. We've said what an initial sequent looks like, and we've given the rules of inference. derivations in the sequent calculus are inductively generated from these: each derivation either is an initial sequent on its own, or consists of one or two derivations followed by an inference. Definition. Title: L K derivation. An L K -derivation of a sequent S is a finite tree of sequents satisfying the following conditions: Begin list. Next item. The topmost sequents of the tree are initial sequents. Next item. The bottommost sequent of the tree is S . Next item. Every sequent in the tree except S is a premise of a correct application of an inference rule whose conclusion stands directly below that sequent in the tree. We then say that S is the end-sequent of the derivation and that S is derivable in the sequent calculus L K (or the sequent calculus L K -derivable). Example. Every initial sequent, e.g., antecedent containing formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C is a derivation. We can obtain a new derivation from this by applying, say, the left weakening rule, Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula A, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta End proof diagram. The rule, however, is meant to be general: we can replace the formula A in the rule with any sentence, e.g., also with formula D . If the premise matches our initial sequent antecedent containing formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C , that means that both Gamma and capital Delta are just formula C , and the conclusion would then be antecedent containing first formula D, then formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C . So, the following is a derivation: Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula D, then formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C End proof diagram. We can now apply another rule, say left exchange rule , which allows us to switch two sentences on the left. So, the following is also a correct derivation: Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula D, then formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C Rule label: left exchange rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula C, then formula D; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C End proof diagram. In this application of the rule, which was given as Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing first Gamma, then formula A, then formula B, and finally capital Pi; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta Rule label: left exchange rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first Gamma, then formula B, then formula A, and finally capital Pi; sequent arrow; succedent containing capital Delta, followed by a printed trailing comma with no following formula Source disclosure. Preserve and speak the printed trailing comma as having no following formula, then disclose that it appears to be stray punctuation. End proof diagram. both Gamma and capital Pi were empty, capital Delta is formula C , and the roles of formula A and formula B are played by formula D and formula C , respectively. In much the same way, we also see that Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing formula D; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula D Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula C, then formula D; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula D End proof diagram. is a derivation. Now we can take these two derivations, and combine them using right conjunction rule . That rule was Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A Premise. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula B Rule label: right conjunction rule. From the two preceding branches, infer. antecedent containing Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then the conjunction of formula A and formula B End proof diagram. In our case, the premises must match the last sequents of the derivations ending in the premises. That means that Gamma is first formula C, then formula D , capital Delta is empty, formula A is formula C and formula B is formula D . So the conclusion, if the inference should be correct, is antecedent containing first formula C, then formula D; sequent arrow; succedent containing the conjunction of formula C and formula D . From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first formula D, then formula C; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula C Rule label: left exchange rule. From the two preceding branches, infer. antecedent containing first formula C, then formula D; sequent arrow; succedent containing the conjunction of formula C and formula D End proof diagram. Of course, we can also reverse the premises, then formula A would be formula D and formula B would be formula C . Begin proof diagram. Give an L K -derivation for the sequent antecedent containing the conjunction of formula A and formula B; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A . We begin by writing the desired end-sequent at the bottom of the derivation. Begin proof diagram. Blank premise slot. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing the conjunction of formula A and formula B; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A End proof diagram. Next, we need to figure out what kind of inference could have a lower sequent of this form. This could be a structural rule, but it is a good idea to start by looking for a logical rule. The only logical connective occurring in the lower sequent is conjunction , so we're looking for an conjunction rule, and since the conjunction symbol occurs in the antecedent, we're looking at the left conjunction rule. Begin proof diagram. Blank premise slot. Rule label: left conjunction rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing the conjunction of formula A and formula B; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A End proof diagram. There are two options for what could have been the upper sequent of the left conjunction rule inference: we could have an upper sequent of antecedent containing formula A; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A , or of antecedent containing formula B; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A . Clearly, antecedent containing formula A; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A is an initial sequent (which is a good thing), while antecedent containing formula B; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A is not derivable in general. We fill in the upper sequent: Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing formula A; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A Rule label: left conjunction rule. Give an L K -derivation of the sequent antecedent containing for some variable x, the negation of formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing the negation of for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x . When dealing with quantifiers, we have to make sure not to violate the eigenvariable condition, and sometimes this requires us to play around with the order of carrying out certain inferences. In general, it helps to try and take care of rules subject to the eigenvariable condition first (they will be lower down in the finished proof). Also, it is a good idea to try and look ahead and try to guess what the initial sequent might look like. In our case, it will have to be something like antecedent containing formula A with argument constant a; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant a . That means that when we are “reversing” the quantifier rules, we will have to pick the same term—what we will call constant a —for both the universal quantifier and the existential quantifier rule. If we picked different terms for each rule, we would end up with something like antecedent containing formula A with argument constant a; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant b , which, of course, is not derivable. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for some variable x, the negation of formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing the negation of for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x End proof diagram. We could either carry out the left existential quantifier rule or the right negation rule. Since the left existential quantifier rule is subject to the eigenvariable condition, it's a good idea to take care of it sooner rather than later, so we'll do that one first. Begin proof diagram. Blank premise slot. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for some variable x, the negation of formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing the negation of for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x End proof diagram. At this point, our only option is to carry out the left universal quantifier rule. Since this rule is not subject to the eigenvariable restriction, we're in the clear. Remember, we want to try and obtain an initial sequent (of the form antecedent containing formula A with argument constant a; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant a ), so we should choose constant a as our argument for formula A when we apply the rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument constant a Rule label: left negation rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing for some variable x, the negation of formula A with argument variable x; sequent arrow; succedent containing the negation of for every variable x, formula A with argument variable x End proof diagram. It is important, especially when dealing with quantifiers, to double check at this point that the eigenvariable condition has not been violated. listen_text: Editorial note. This section collects the definitions of the provability relation and consistency for natural deduction. Section. Proof-Theoretic Notions. Explanation. Just as we've defined a number of important semantic notions (validity, entailment, satisfiability), we now define corresponding proof-theoretic notions. These are not defined by appeal to satisfaction of sentences in structures, but by appeal to the derivability or nonderivability of certain sequents. It was an important discovery that these notions coincide. That they do is the content of the soundness and completeness theorem. Definition. Title: Theorems. A sentence formula A is a theorem if there is a derivation in the sequent calculus L K of the sequent antecedent containing no formulas; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A . We write no premises syntactically derives formula A if formula A is a theorem and no premises does not syntactically derive formula A if it is not. Definition. Title: derivability. A sentence formula A is derivable from a set of sentences Gamma , Gamma syntactically derives formula A , iff there is a finite subset Gamma sub zero is a subset of Gamma and a sequence Gamma sub zero prime of the sentences in Gamma sub zero such that the sequent calculus L K derives antecedent containing Gamma sub zero prime; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A . listen_text: Section. derivation with identity. derivations with identity require additional initial sequents and inference rules. Definition. Title: Initial sequents for identity sign . If term t is a closed term, then antecedent containing the empty sequence; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t is identical to term t is an initial sequent. The rules for identity sign are ( term t sub one and term t sub two are closed terms): Rule definition. Premise. antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t sub one Rule label: identity sign . From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t sub two End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t sub two Rule label: identity sign . From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t sub one End displayed proof. Example. If lowercase s and term t are closed terms, then first lowercase s is identical to term t, then formula A with argument lowercase s syntactically derives formula A with argument term t : Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing formula A with argument lowercase s; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument lowercase s Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first lowercase s is identical to term t, then formula A with argument lowercase s; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument lowercase s Rule label: identity sign . From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first lowercase s is identical to term t, then formula A with argument lowercase s; sequent arrow; succedent containing formula A with argument term t End proof diagram. This may be familiar as the principle of substitutability of identicals, or Leibniz' Law. the sequent calculus L K proves that identity sign is symmetric and transitive: Begin proof diagram. Premise. antecedent containing no formulas; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub one Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub two; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub one Rule label: identity sign . From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub two; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub two is identical to term t sub one End displayed proof. Premise. antecedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub two; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub two Rule label: left weakening rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first term t sub two is identical to term t sub three, then term t sub one is identical to term t sub two; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub two Rule label: identity sign . From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first term t sub two is identical to term t sub three, then term t sub one is identical to term t sub two; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub three Rule label: left exchange rule. From the preceding branch, infer. antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then term t sub two is identical to term t sub three; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t sub one is identical to term t sub three End proof diagram. In the derivation on the left, the formula variable x is identical to term t sub one is our formula A with argument variable x . listen_text: Section. Soundness with identity. Proposition. the sequent calculus L K with initial sequents and rules for identity is sound. Proof. Initial sequents of the form antecedent containing the empty sequence; sequent arrow; succedent containing term t is identical to term t are valid, since for every structure M , structure M satisfies term t is identical to term t . (Note that we assume the term t to be closed, i.e., it contains no variables, so variable assignments are irrelevant). Suppose the last inference in a derivation is identity sign . Then the premise is antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t sub one and the conclusion is antecedent containing first term t sub one is identical to term t sub two, then Gamma; sequent arrow; succedent containing first capital Delta, then formula A with argument term t sub two . Consider a structure M . We need to show that the conclusion is valid, i.e., if structure M satisfies term t sub one is identical to term t sub two and structure M satisfies Gamma , then either structure M satisfies formula C for some formula C is a member of capital Delta or structure M satisfies formula A with argument term t sub two . By induction hypothesis, the premise is valid. This means that if structure M satisfies term t sub one is identical to term t sub two and structure M satisfies Gamma either (a) for some formula C is a member of capital Delta , structure M satisfies formula C or (b) structure M satisfies formula A with argument term t sub one . In case (a) we are done. Consider case (b). Let lowercase s be a variable assignment with s applied to variable x is identical to the value of term t sub one in structure M . By the proposition linking satisfaction of a sentence with truth in a structure, M, under variable assignment lowercase s, satisfies formula A with argument term t sub one . Since variable assignment lowercase s agrees with variable assignment lowercase s except possibly at variable x , by the proposition on assignment extensionality for formulas, structure M, under variable assignment lowercase s, satisfies formula A with argument variable x . since structure M satisfies term t sub one is identical to term t sub two , we have the value of term t sub one in structure M is identical to the value of term t sub two in structure M , and hence s applied to variable x is identical to the value of term t sub two in structure M . By applying the proposition on assignment extensionality for formulas again, we also have structure M, under variable assignment lowercase s, satisfies formula A with argument term t sub two . By the proposition linking satisfaction of a sentence with truth in a structure, M satisfies formula A with argument term t sub two .
